trace.msg: Let's look at this puzzle carefully. I'll only move when I can explain why.

Going to (4,4,1) would leave number 2 unreachable without crossing a higher number; going to (6,6,1) would leave number 2 unreachable without crossing a higher number (and 1 more option fails too). So the line goes to (2,6,1).
Number 2 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going to (2,7,4) would leave number 3 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes to (4,7,2).
Number 3 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going to (6,7,4) would leave number 4 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes to (6,6,1).
Number 4 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going to (4,4,1) would leave number 5 unreachable without crossing a higher number; going to (6,2,1) would leave number 5 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes to (7,4,2).
Number 5 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Number 6 is only reachable this way.
Going to (7,4,6) would force the line onto number 9 before its turn. So the line goes to (6,6,7).
Number 7 is next and right here, so the line takes it.
Going to (7,4,6) would force the line onto number 9 before its turn. So the line goes to (6,2,7).
Going to (7,2,6) leaves no safe move afterwards; going to (6,1,6), the next move is forced and the line gets stuck at cell (4,1,6). So the line goes to (4,2,7).
The line must go to (4,1,6): to (2,2,7) is number 16, which comes later; to (4,4,7) is number 23, which comes later.
Going to (2,1,6) would leave number 9 unreachable without crossing a higher number. So the line goes to (6,1,6).
The line must go to (7,2,6): to (6,1,4) is number 10, which comes later.
Cell (7,4,6) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (7,4,4).
Going to (4,1,2) would force the line onto number 15 before its turn; going to (6,2,1) would turn number 11 into a dead-end pocket with no way out. So the line goes to (7,2,2).
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (6,2,1).
Cell (4,4,1) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (2,4,1).
Going to (1,4,2) would force the line onto number 18 before its turn. So the line goes to (2,2,1).
I can't rule out to (2,1,2) or to (1,2,2) yet, so I'll make an educated guess: to (2,1,2).

Contradiction! Every way forward fails: going to (1,2,6), the next 2 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (1,2,2); going to (2,4,7) would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order). So my guess (to (2,1,2) from cell (2,2,1)) was wrong, so the line must go to (1,2,2).
Going to (1,4,2) would force the line onto number 18 before its turn; going to (1,2,4), the next move is forced and the line gets stuck at cell (1,2,6). So the line goes to (2,1,2).
Cell (4,1,2) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (4,1,4).
Going to (1,2,4), the next 6 moves are forced and the line gets stuck at cell (2,7,6). So the line goes to (2,1,6).
Going to (1,2,6) would leave both cell (1,2,4) and number 16 needing the line next, and it can't do both. So the line goes to (2,2,7).
Going to (2,4,7) would force the two-exit cells to link up into a loop (or put the numbers out of order). So the line goes to (1,2,6).
The line must go to (1,2,4): to (1,4,6) is number 22, which comes later.
Cell (1,4,2) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (1,6,2).
Going to (1,6,6) would force the line onto number 22 before its turn. So the line goes to (2,7,4).
Going to (2,7,6) leaves no safe move afterwards. So the line goes to (4,7,4).
Cell (6,7,4) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (6,7,6).
Going to (2,7,6) leaves no safe move afterwards. So the line goes to (4,6,7).
The line must go to (2,6,7): to (4,4,7) is number 23, which comes later.
Cell (2,7,6) has only two exits, so the line must pass through it now.
Only one free cell next to the line, so it goes to (1,6,6).
Every cell is covered and the numbers are in order. Case closed!
I grow a search tree: my policy network suggests moves, a trained value head judge them. 56 simulations per move.
One of my simulated futures reached the end after 36 simulations. Following it!
Let evolution do the work: 24 random lines compete, the fittest breed and mutate.

Generation 7: fitness 54/54. The best line covers 54 cells.
Generation 7: a perfect line evolved! Every cell covered.
Feeling lucky! Before every move I'll play 24 random futures and bet on the move that survives most often.

Tried 48 futures: 4% survive going to (4,7,2) (best covers 24%); to (2,7,4) 0%.
Tried 48 futures: 0% survive going to (6,6,1) (best covers 24%); to (6,7,4) 0%.

Tried 48 futures: 4% survive going to (6,6,7) (best covers 67%); to (7,4,6) 0%.
Tried 48 futures: 92% survive going to (6,2,7) (best covers 67%); to (7,4,6) 0%.
Tried 72 futures: 100% survive going to (4,2,7) (best covers 69%); to (7,2,6) 0%; to (6,1,6) 0%.
Tried 48 futures: 100% survive going to (6,1,6) (best covers 69%); to (2,1,6) 0%.
Tried 48 futures: 100% survive going to (7,4,6) (best covers 72%); to (7,2,4) 0%.
Jackpot! A future covers the whole board. Cashing in!
Let x(cell, step) mean 'this cell is step number <step> of the line'. 54 cells x 54 steps, minus everything that's impossible at a glance.
Encoded 7,385 variables and 20,203 clauses in 0.01 s (2,109 position variables survive the pruning).
Solver found a model in 0.03 s. Decoding it into a line...
Q.E.D. Every clause is satisfied.
